Measured on PR #545 run 34685410794 by reading runner_name back from the API rather than from the workflow file, three of this repository's own jobs reported `runner=GitHub Actions <n>` with `labels=ubuntu-latest`. refuted_claims: That seven macOS/Windows legs remain -- the branch said six, in five places. grep prints six LINES because lint.yml contributes one line and two legs, and the count predated this branch's own rewrite of that matrix.

That reading the object form's `group` alongside its `labels` is correct. A runner GROUP is not a label: a group named `ubuntu-runners` reported as a hosted runner, and the fleet control caught it on the first run.
That the branch moved 32 declarations. 33, re-derived by counting hosted-Linux labels present at the base and absent at HEAD; 32 was the conversion script's own report.
That a vacuity floor of 20 is a guard. Measured at 48, so more than half the fleet jobs could have been deleted before it noticed. The floor is now 40.

That actions/cache degrades on a clean-room runner and should be removed (lane 1). It talks to GitHub's cache service over the network and works from a self-hosted runner; this branch changes nothing about it.

That moving ci.yml's job breaks its real-sudo test (lane 1). Failing loudly where the capability is absent is the DESIGNED behaviour -- FORJAR_REQUIRE_SUDO_TESTS turns a skip into a panic, which is why the comment citing GitHub's documented environment was removed and only the switch was kept.

five of lane 2's nine findings were graded `asserted` rather than measured, which is what a NO WRITES brief costs: a lane cannot run the parser it is reasoning about. Four of those five were true and are now fixtures.

falsification.test: ten cases. Four are the invariants; five are controls built from a lane's `asserted` findings, each a fixture feeding one shape that hid a hosted runner from the parser -- the object form of runs-on, a hosted label in another case, a matrix key not named runner/os, an expression nested in a runs-on list, and a fleet job that must NOT be mistaken for a hosted one; the tenth counts the three jobs whose runner is chosen by a reusable workflow in another repository, which no case here can read.
falsification.reverted: four targeted mutations over the COMMITTED tree, each restored by name from HEAD, every run --no-fail-fast. M1 (one Linux job back to ubuntu-latest), M2 (a hosted leg added) and M3 (`runs-on: self-hosted` without a pool) each kill exactly one case. M4 blinds `push_labels` and KILLS SIX OF THE TEN -- every case that reads through the parser -- which is the right answer and not a clean kill: the four survivors all assert an ABSENCE, and a blinded parser reports nothing hosted, so they pass while measuring nothing. That is precisely what the_parser_finds_the_runners_that_are_there exists to catch. An earlier draft claimed four single kills and no collateral; that was true of the four-case suite the round grew to ten. `git status --porcelain -- .github tests` is 0 lines after every mutation.

systems: Nix (builders are declared in nix.conf and a build that cannot reach one fails rather than falling back)
Bazel remote execution (the execution platform is part of the action key, so a local and a remote runner are never interchangeable by accident)
GitLab CI (runner tags are matched explicitly and an untagged job is refused when the project requires tags)
Buildkite (agent tags are queried and a step with no matching queue waits visibly rather than running somewhere else)
crux.verdict: accept(every surveyed system makes WHERE a job runs an explicit, checked property rather than a default, and three of the four refuse or block rather than silently substituting a runner. GitHub Actions is the outlier: `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` is the path of least resistance, it always works, and nothing in a green check says which machine produced it -- which is why this repository spent hosted runners for months without noticing. forjar cannot change the default, so it does what GitLab does with required tags: it makes the property checkable and checks it. Where forjar is WORSE than Buildkite: seven legs still have no fleet queue at all and are simply counted, where Buildkite would block visibly. Where it is better than a lint rule: the check reads the same YAML GitHub reads, so a hosted runner hidden in a matrix or in the object form of runs-on is a finding rather than prose a grep never saw.)
